new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable. The modern source (Hargus & Da Conceição 1999) reports this impressionistically and notes that certain verb forms carry an unexpected (non-penultimate) accent, e.g. [áuda] 'you used to eat' vs expected [aúdi]. The same penultimate rule is stated categorically in the older grammars: Junod 1896 p. 39 'l'accentuation.. tombe presque toujours sur l'avant-dernière syllabe. Exemple : masíku, les jours; bunyamenyáme, minutie'; Pinheiro 1897 p. 12 'Em geral o accento recahe na penultima syllaba'; Torre do Valle 1906 p. 19 'O accento tonico colloca-se em geral sobre a penultima syllaba'. Junod p. 32 adds that the accented (penultimate) vowel is generally long.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Hargus & Da Conceição 1999 p. 38: 'unpredictable accent in certain verbs' ([áuda] 'you used to eat', initial accent, vs expected penult). Junod 1896 §22-23 pp. 39-40: monosyllables either become disyllabic (tána 'come'), become clitics, or join a following/preceding monosyllable into one phonetic unit with the accent on the penult of the group (tiko dá nga 'my country'); some monosyllabic adverbs (le 'there', la 'here', descriptive adverbs) bear an accent; plural imperatives and locatives in -an/-en/-in (fambán 'go!', misabén 'on the ground', nkhinsín 'in the valley') sound final-stressed, but Junod calls this 'exception qu'apparente' because the full forms are -ani/-eni/-ini, so the accent is still penultimate. Torre do Valle 1906 p. 19: a monosyllable throws the accent onto the last syllable of the preceding word (or onto the infinitive particle ku). Junod §57 also notes a rising vs falling 'accent' distinguishing miri 'trees' from miri 'body' (i.e. tone).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including clitic groups, per Junod §22); statements are about isolated words/citation forms and connected speech alike. Hargus & Da Conceição explicitly say the phonetic correlates of the penultimate prominence were not determined, and they mention pitch effects of breathy (depressor) consonants; the language also has tone (Junod §57 minimal pair), so the 'stress' is the usual Southern-Bantu penultimate prominence/lengthening rather than a contrastive stress system.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Ronga proper (rong1268). Hargus & Da Conceição 1999 describe the speech of one consultant, Manuel Da Conceição, who grew up in Maputo city and calls his variety Xi-zronga (the downtown-Maputo dialect, per his own dialect list on pp. 28-30 of the same volume); Junod 1896, Pinheiro 1897 and Torre do Valle 1906 describe the Ronga of the Lourenço Marques (Delagoa Bay) district, i.e. the same language. Glottolog has no separate code for these dialects that I could verify.

new_statements.quote: Generally, the Caffre dialects are composed of words very short, sweet, and sonorous, as they are very rich in vowels, simple, and open, pronounced with a sharp accent on the penultimate syllable; not through the nose nor guttural, with the exception of the Hottentot's dialect [...] The dialect of the Caffres of Santa Luzia river, in the territories of the King Capela Inyack and Matola, and at the Bay of Sourenço Marques, is derived from the dialect Makove, having all of them their common origin in the language of Hottentots; they keep the nasal sound as well as the guttural, but they differ in the accentuation and termination of the words.

new_statements.relation_note: The general penultimate-accent statement matches the catalog (fixed penult) and Hargus & Da Conceição 1999 / Junod 1896 / Pinheiro 1897 / Torre do Valle 1906, but it is made for the Mozambican 'Caffre dialects' collectively, not for Ronga in particular; the only sentence about the Ronga area (Delagoa Bay) says merely that its accentuation differs from 'Makove', with no placement given. Treat as weak, non-specific corroboration rather than an independent Ronga description. The Glottolog tag 'grammar sketch' overstates the item: it is a three-page letter listing older Angolan grammars and characterising Mozambican dialects impressionistically.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A generic 1864 travel-letter claim that the 'Caffre' (Bantu) dialects of Mozambique are pronounced with a sharp accent on the penultimate syllable. The Delagoa Bay / Lourenço Marques dialect (printed 'Sourenço Marques'; the Inyack-Matola-Santa Luzia area, i.e. the Ronga-speaking country) is then said to 'differ in the accentuation and termination of the words' from the 'Makove' dialect it is supposedly derived from, without saying how. No Ronga-specific rule, no examples, no phonetic detail.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement; the only qualification is that the Lourenço Marques dialect 'differs in the accentuation' from Makove, unexplained. The letter is a pre-scientific overview (it also derives the Bantu dialects from Hottentot and from Arabic), so its claims carry little weight.
new_statements.identity_note: Figanière 1864 does not name Ronga; it speaks of 'the Caffre dialects' of Portuguese East Africa generally and of 'the dialect of the Caffres of Santa Luzia river, in the territories of the King Capela Inyack and Matola, and at the Bay of Sourenço [= Lourenço] Marques' (the Delagoa Bay area where Ronga is spoken), which it says derives from 'Makove'. It is a pre-scientific overview, not a description of a specific Ronga dialect.
